paper_title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) generate text autoregressively, requiring full forward pass of the model for every generated token. While this serial dependency ensures high-quality text generation, it also imposes significant computational bottleneck, and poorly exploits the capacity of modern hardware, as illustrated in recent studies on LLM inference efficiency [33, 29, 23, 15]. Speculative decoding [25, 36] addresses this serial bottleneck by configuring the LLM to act as target model that verifies, in parallel, sequence of token proposals (a draft) submitted by smaller drafter model. The verification process applies rejection sampling to the draft to ensure that the target model distribution is respected, guaranteeing no quality loss [25]. Since verification is parallelized over the draft, speculative decoding can unlock faster generation speeds. The generation speed of speculative decoding is reduced by drafting latency and is increased by the tokens per forward (TPF), denoting the expected number of tokens committed per speculative round. TPF is determined by draft quality: the number of draft tokens that align with the target models distribution. Larger drafters can improve draft quality, but often introduce additional latency that offsets these gains [27]. Parallel drafters [32, 26] achieve low draft latency by generating the entire draft in single forward pass. However, modeling the dependencies between draft tokens generated in parallel is challenging for drafters, impairing draft quality. To support draft quality, parallel drafters tend to rely on two key mechanisms: feature encoding, which conditions the drafter on encoded hidden states of the target model [6, 40], and causal heads, which apply lightweight autoregressive adjustments to the parallel draft posteriors [8, 22]. However, this work reveals flaws in both mechanisms. Feature encoding in state-of-the-art parallel drafters suffers from three limitations: (i) Residual mixing: Standard feature encoding [6, 22] uses dense projection matrix that mixes representations across the hidden state dimension of the target model, an effect that this paper shows produces less useful contextual features. (ii) Memory-less encoding: Existing encoders only encode the drafters context, ignoring the useful features present within previously rejected proposals. (iii) Uniform layer selection: Existing encoders heuristically select hidden states uniformly throughout the depth of the target model, without regard to which layers are the most useful for drafting [40]. Existing causal heads are also limited: they either lack expressivity [8] or cannot make global vocabulary corrections [22]. To address these limitations, this paper introduces DNeo, parallel draft architecture that pairs structure-preserving feature encoding with expressive causal adjustments. Its architectural components are designed to enhance LLM generation speed by improving the expected TPF. Contributions. The paper makes three contributions: 1. It shows that existing feature encoding suffers from residual mixing (Section 5.4.1), and replaces the dense encoder with Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), lightweight mixture of target layers that improves TPF by +0.6 over dense encoding (Sections 4.1 and 5.4). It also shows that encoding uniformly spaced hidden states harms draft quality, and introduces the DNeo protocol, which isolates the contextually richer later half of the target model (Section 4.5). 2. It shows that previously rejected draft tokens contain useful features, and introduces rejection memory, which equips the drafter with cross-attention to these features and improves TPF by +0.17 over memory-less drafter (Section 4.3). It also introduces the fused DNeo causal head, which combines two common causal heads [8, 22] in latent space and improves draft quality over both heads in isolation (Section 4.2), and streamlines the drafter with prefix-only attention (Section 4.4). 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. All Rights Reserved. 2 DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding Figure 2: Draft quality comparison. Tokens per forward (τ ) over the test-set (Section 5.1), using official SGLang inference implementations. DNeo dominates existing methods in draft quality. 3. Through extensive experiments in realistic serving settings with SGLang, it shows that DNeos higher draft quality translates into faster generation than state-of-the-art parallel drafters on common benchmarks outside its training distribution (Section 5). On chain-of-thought workloads [28] with Qwen3-4B [37], DNeo generates up to 30% faster than DFlash-2 [22] and delivers 16% higher throughput at batch size 32  (Fig. 1)  .

sections.title: 2 Background
sections.content: This section reviews the two foundations of DNeo: the verification process of speculative decoding, which ensures that generation quality does not degrade, and parallel drafters, which enable lowlatency draft generation. Speculative Decoding. Autoregressive (AR) language models generate single token per forward pass, making inference latency directly proportional to output length. Speculative decoding [25, 36] can accelerate AR inference by replacing serial generation with parallel verification phase. At each speculative round, the smaller draft model q() proposes draft of draft tokens (ˆx1, . . . , ˆxb) q(ˆx1, ), . . . , q(ˆxb, ), to be verified by the target model p() in single parallel forward pass p(ˆx1, . . . , ˆxb), akin to the prefill of prompt. token ˆxi from the draft is accepted, i.e., committed to the final output, with probability Pr[accept ˆxi] min(1, p(ˆxi, )/q(ˆxi, )), which intuitively scales in proportion to the quality of the proposed draft token ˆxi. The first rejection at position τ discards all subsequent tokens (ˆxτ +1, . . . , ˆxb) regardless of their quality, and ˆxτ is replaced with bonus token xbonus sampled from the correction distribution xbonus norm(max(p() q(ˆxτ ), 0)). This criterion ensures that the committed block (ˆx1, . . . , ˆxτ 1, xbonus) is theoretically sampled from the target posterior p(), making decoding lossless [25]. Each speculative round thus commits τ tokens, at the cost of the drafting time tdraft and the verification time tverify; we refer to the expected τ as the tokens per forward (TPF), and Fig. 2 compares it across drafters. The average latency per generated token is then, time token (s) = tdraft + tverify τ , meaning that latency per token is reduced by increasing τ through improved draft quality, as long as the speculative overhead tdraft + tverify does not proportionally increase. Raising τ without proportionally raising this overhead is the goal of every component of DNeo (Section 4). 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. All Rights Reserved. 3 DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding Parallel Token Prediction. Parallel token prediction has been an area of significant research interest [13, 14, 39] for its potential to reduce LLM inference latency, and support fast speculative drafting [9, 32]. The most common form of parallel drafters, masked LMs [31], take as input block of masked token embeddings [m]1, . . . , [m]b, the masked block, and generate set of token predictions: (ˆx1, . . . , ˆxb) qparallel , x1, . . . , xn } {z prefix [m]1, . . . , [m]b {z } masked block (1) from the contextualized hidden state at each masked position. Typically, parallel drafters attend to the clean context xctx = (x1, . . . , xn) of committed tokens, drawn from vocabulary V, via cross-attention, and perform bidirectional self-attention over the learned masked embeddings [6]. During drafting, this attention structure enables contextual information to be absorbed into masked embeddings, while self-attention is designed to support self consistent draft blocks [6]; though Section 4.4 revisits this second choice. Supplying parallel models with rich contextual representations, and ensuring that tokens generated in parallel (ˆx1, . . . , ˆxb) respect left-to-right consistency prove to be critical for improving parallel generation quality [8, 20, 6]. Architectural components that support these two goals are reviewed in the next section.

sections.title: 3 Architectural Components of Parallel Drafters
sections.content: Recent parallel token drafters, leveraging the framework of speculative decoding, introduce several architectural components (see Table 1), three of which are directly relevant to DNeo: (i) target feature encoding, (ii) causal heads, and (iii) rejection attention [6, 8, 40, 22, 41]. Each component addresses weakness of parallel drafting, and each leaves limitation that DNeo addresses (Section 4). Target Feature Encoding. Feature encoding extracts rich target model features of the clean context xctx = (x1, . . . , xn), in order to supply the drafter with representations that improve its ability to make high quality predictions [6, 22, 8, 40]. During prefill and verification, hidden states h(l1), . . . ,h(lc) from subset of target layers l1, . . . , lc are concatenated1 and down-projected into the drafters dh dimensional hidden space. The standard encoding approach is dense linear encoder Fc Rcdhdh fi = encdense(xi) RMSNorm[Fc(h(l1) h(lc) )], (2) producing the context feature encoding fi of the token xi xctx. Context features ( f1, . . . , fn) are then used by draft models to compute contextual key-value cache (Kj ctx) at every draft layer ℓj of drafter with layers, ctx, Kj ctx = ( f1, . . . , fn), and ctx = ( f1, . . . , fn), (3) via the drafters key-value projections . During drafting, masked positions absorb rich prefix information via cross-attention to context features  (Fig. 4)  , producing draft quality improvements (+40% larger τ ; [6]). However, two choices of this design limit the drafter. Second, the layers l1, . . . , lc are spaced uniformly across the target model, regardless of their usefulness for drafting. Sections 4.1 and 4.5 revisit these two choices. Causal Heads. Parallel draft models have been shown to suffer from phenomenon known as suffix decay [8]. By default, parallel drafter backbones generate the draft block (ˆx1, . . . , ˆxb) in single forward pass, meaning that each draft token does not condition on draft tokens sampled in other parts of the block, leading to left-to-right, or causal, incoherence of the draft [8, 17, 19]. Draft tokens further away from the prefix have fewer directly preceding sampled tokens to condition on, causing draft quality to degrade with draft position: this is suffix decay [8]. Suffix decay in parallel models is generally addressed via causal head, popularized by DSpark [8]. Typically, causal heads are parametrized by low rank matrix Wr, qparallel (ˆxj) softmax(zj + Wr(1[ˆxj1]) ) } {z Causal Head , (4) which applies correction to the backbone logits zj RV at each draft position j. The adjusted posterior is computed for all indexes (1 . . . b) in left-to-right manner, ensuring that each sampled token ˆxj is causally consistent with its predecessor ˆxj1; this sequential pass is the main cost of causal head. DFlash-2 [22] extends this design with more expressive bilinear score head, which re-scores only the top-k candidates of the backbone (Section 4.2), and with 2-tap convolutions, which mix each masked state with that of its left neighbor before and after every attention and MLP operation  (Fig. 3)  . However, Wr conditions only on the previous token through low-rank linear map, while the score head cannot promote tokens outside the top-k candidates; Section 4.2 combines the strengths of both. Rejection Attention. Conventionally, state-of-the-art parallel drafter architectures do not leverage draft information from previous speculative rounds [6, 8, 22, 40]. This memory-less property limits the prediction accuracy of drafters in online settings (Section 4.3). sections.title: 4 DNeo Architecture
sections.content: The outline of the DNeo architecture is shown in Fig. 3. The key innovations introduced aim to increase τ , the number of tokens committed per speculative round, without increasing the speculative overhead tdraft + tverify (Section 2). Each innovation addresses limitation identified in Section 3: MoFA removes residual mixing from feature encoding (Section 4.1), the fused causal head improves the expressivity of existing heads (Section 4.2), rejection memory lets the drafter exploit rejected 2Via Hadamard product 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. All Rights Reserved. 6 DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding proposals (Section 4.3), DNeo cross-attention removes redundant computation from the backbone (Section 4.4), and the DNeo feature selector encodes the most useful target layers (Section 4.5). 4.1 Feature Encoding Existing literature has not yet isolated which target hidden states are most important for parallel drafters, nor adequately explored how different encoding operations impact τ . This section proposes Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), feature encoder that avoids the residual mixing of the standard dense encoder Fc (Section 3), yields superior τ , and makes the importance of each target hidden state interpretable. MoFA fusion. Each of the selected hidden states h(l1) is assigned an importance scalar u1, . . . , uc, collectively parametrized by softmax vector u1, . . . , uc = softmax(w1, . . . , wc) of scalar weights. Target hidden states are weighted by importance to produce the fused feature , . . . ,h(lc) fi = EncMoFA(xi) softmax(w1, . . . , wc) (h(l1) = u1h(l1) + u2h(l2) + + uch(lc) , , . . . ,h(lc) ), (5) (6) defining the differentiable encoding operation EncMoFA(), whose learned weights we call the MoFA gate. Two properties motivate this form. First, each uk scales an entire hidden state, so every coordinate of fi combines only the same coordinate across target layers: MoFA performs no residual mixing by construction (Section 5.4.1). Second, the softmax turns the weights into distribution over target layers, an attention over the depth of the target model that gives MoFA its name, so each learned scalar uk can be read directly as the importance of layer lk; Section 4.5 uses these importances to select layers. The fused feature fi is re-used by all drafter layers, distinguishing MoFA from the per-layer features of DFlare [40] and keeping the encoder minimal. Importantly, MoFA produces consistent increases in τ relative to the standard dense feature encoder (+16%, Section 5.4.1) while using 0.05% as many encoding parameters (Section 5). Practical considerations. MoFA assumes that the hidden state dimensions of the draft and target model are equal, d(drafter) = d(target) = dh, since it passes target coordinates to the drafter unchanged; this assumption is consistent with the parallel drafters of frontier open LLMs [12, 11]. However, much like the dense feature encoder, MoFA can be extended to the general case where d(drafter) = d(target) by setting the input dimension of the drafters key-value matrices equal to d(target). faithful reproduction of structure-preserving encoding (i.e., MoFA, DFlare) requires that the model hidden dimensions are set equal to one another [40].

sections.content: Recall that causal head corrects the backbone logits zj left to right, conditioning each draft position on the token sampled before it, to counter suffix decay (Section 3). The DSpark causal head Wr [8] is limited in expressivity, conditioning solely on the one-hot draft predecessor 1[ˆxj1] with low rank linear adjustment. Instead, the score head of DFlash-2 [22], which we denote DF2, computes more expressive logit adjustments zj(ˆxj ˆxj1) } {z logit correction (11) = DF2(ˆxj, ˆxj1) [W 1[ˆxj1] h(ℓm) ] ˆxj {z } } (1r) {z (1r) (7) 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. The logit correction zj(ˆxj ˆxj1) is added to the logit vector zj indexed by proposal ˆxj, parallelized over all draft positions. However, the DF2 head is applied only to the top-k (k = 16) logits across the draft, preventing the head from making global vocabulary adjustments. Instead, DNeo uses the DF2 head architecture to improve the expressivity of the DSpark causal head Wr, by combining the outputs of the two heads in their shared rank-r latent space before up-projecting to the full vocabulary: DNeohead(ˆxj1) Wup {z } (rV) (cid:16) αj (cid:2)W (1[ˆxj1]) h(ℓm) {z Dense DF2 Head (1r) (cid:3) Q[V] } + βj Wdown {z } (1[xj1] DSpark Head (Vr) (cid:17) , ) (8) with position-dependent learned scalar weights αj, βj R, and Q[V] RVr denoting the low-rank query embeddings of the full vocabulary. Each element of this design addresses limitation of one head. The DNeo head evaluates the DFlash-2 operation against the full vocabulary V, rather than the top-k candidates, so that its context-aware correction becomes global: zj( ˆxj1) = DNeohead(ˆxj1) RV. The latent fusion lets this context-aware term enrich the low-rank code of the DSpark head, which Wup then maps to the full vocabulary, and the weights αj, βj let the balance between the two terms vary along the draft block. The DNeo head defines the corrected posterior qDNeo (ˆxj ˆxj1, ) = softmax(zj + DNeohead(ˆxj1)), (9) and applies the correction left-to-right throughout the draft block following DSpark [8], so that each sampled token remains consistent with its predecessor (Section 3).

sections.title: 4.3 Rejection Memory
sections.content: State-of-the-art parallel drafters utilize encoded context features fi while ignoring features from rejected draft tokens [6, 8, 22, 40]. However, rejected tokens are natural source of additional information for subsequent rounds. Recall that the target model verifies the entire draft in single forward pass (Section 2): its hidden states at the rejected positions are therefore already computed, and these positions overlap those that the next round must draft. DNeo exploits this information with rejection memory, novel and lightweight mechanism with two steps: rejection encoding, which encodes the target states over the rejected postfix, and auxiliary attention, which adds cross-attention connections from the masked block to these encoded rejections, consequently enabling the drafter to condition on recent rejection events. Rejection encoding. At speculative round t, the draft ˆx1, . . . , ˆxb is verified, yielding an accepted prefix (x1, . . . , xj) and rejected postfix (ˆxj+1, . . . , ˆxb). Using the same MoFA encoder for both (Section 4.1), context features are computed from the accepted prefix: f1, . . . , fj {z } Context features = EncMoFA(x1, . . . , xj), and rejection features are computed from the full rejected postfix: ( ˆfj+1, . . . , ˆfb) } {z Rejection features = EncMoFA(ˆxj+1, . . . , ˆxb), 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. All Rights Reserved. 8 (10) (11) DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding Figure 4: DNeo Attention mask. Mask assumes block-size = 3 across three drafting rounds. DNeo omits bidirectional self-attention over the masked block, design we call prefix-only attention (Section 4.4), and performs cross-attention to the rejected states ( ˆf3, . . . , ˆf6). he number of rejection features per round varies based on the prior rounds acceptance length. embedding rich information about the rejected postfix. Sharing the encoder places rejection features in the same space as context features, so the drafter can attend to both with its existing key-value projections and without additional encoding parameters. Auxiliary attention. Rejection features are appended after the masked block, which allows the drafter to distinguish them from prefix features. Auxiliary cross-attention connections are added between masked positions and rejection features (see Fig. 4 for the DNeo attention mask). The input Xt+1 to the draft model at the next round + 1 is: Xt+1 = [ f1, . . . , fj } {z Context features , , xbonus [m]1, . . . , [m]b } {z Masked block ( ˆfj+1, . . . , ˆfb) } {z Rejection features (step t) ], (12) where rejection features act as auxiliary context: they supply key-value states, but do not yield predictions. Auxiliary attention enables information to pass through speculative rounds without directly altering the masked block, distinguishing rejection memory from self-conditioning approaches [13, 34, 5, 41], which fuse previous predictions into the drafters inputs. Keeping these two representations distinct preserves the role of the masked embeddings, and lets each masked position retrieve only the rejected features relevant to it (Section 5.4.3). Practical considerations. Rejection memory introduces serial dependencies between speculative rounds, since Xt+1 depends on the outcome of round t. To avoid train-test mismatches, the drafter must therefore be trained on speculative roll-outs, through on-policy distillation [24, 1] (Section 5.1). In practice, parallel drafter training typically occurs online, alongside LLM post-training, making DNeo compatible with frontier training pipelines [12]. 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. All Rights Reserved. 9 DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding 4.4 Prefix-Only Attention Parallel drafters such as DFlash perform bidirectional self-attention over the masked block (Section 2), so that draft positions can coordinate their predictions. DNeo removes this self-attention: masked positions attend only to context and rejection features  (Fig. 4)  , design we call prefix-only attention. Two observations motivate this choice. First, the dependencies between draft positions that matter most are local and left-to-right, and DNeo already captures them with the 2-tap convolutions of DFlash-2 (Section 3) and with its causal head (Section 4.2). In our experiments, self-attention over the masked block brought no further gain in τ once these mechanisms were in place (Appendix A.4). Second, removing self-attention eliminates the key and value projections over masked positions and shrinks the attention mask, which reduces the DNeo backbone latency (Appendix A.6). 4.5 Layer Selection Protocol Feature encoding typically isolates subset of hidden states among the layers of the target model. By default, layer indices are selected uniformly across the target model: iuniform (1, 2c/c, 3c/c, . . . , (c 1)c/c, c), (13) defining the uniform protocol [6, 40], which provides broad coverage across target model depth, but does not select based on how useful different target layers may be to the drafter. However, interpreting layer importance with the MoFA gate (Appendix A.2), whose weights uk measure the importance of each encoded layer (Section 4.1), reveals that the later half of the target model contains the most important hidden states for drafting (Appendix A.2). This is consistent with the role of depth in transformers: later layers refine the residual stream toward the next-token prediction that the drafter must reproduce, while the first layer preserves the identity of each token. DNeo therefore proposes an adjusted protocol that keeps the first layer and draws the remaining hidden state indices from the second half of the target model: iDNeo (1, c/2 + 2c/2c, c/2 + 3c/2c, . . . , c), (14) defining the DNeo protocol. The DNeo protocol ultimately improves τ over the uniform protocol (Section 5.4.4).

sections.title: 5 Results
sections.content: We now evaluate whether the design choices of Section 4 translate into faster lossless generation: Section 5.2 measures speedups at batch size 1, Section 5.3 measures throughput under concurrency, and Section 5.4 isolates the contribution of each component to τ .

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Design
sections.content: These experiments train several SoTA parallel draft architectures [6, 22, 8] with fixed training conditions (i.e., data, hyperparameters, loss function, target model) for two durations: 100,000 rollouts, which we call experimental training and use for ablations, and 1,600,000 rollouts, which we call full training and use for the main results, with learning rate warmed linearly (0 1e5) over 20, 000 rollouts, then linearly decayed (1e5 0) over the remaining rollouts [4]. Because all parallel drafters share the same data, loss, target model, and training budget, differences in τ and speed isolate the effect of architecture. 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. Main results use batch-size=1, (ablated in Table 3), and block-size = 16. Speedup is measured relative to decode-only AR speed, consistent with present literature [6]. sections.title: 5.2 Decoding Speed
sections.content: Table 2 lists our main results, where each architecture was trained to draft (distillation) for Qwen3-4B. Results show that DNeo dominates SoTA parallel drafters in both draft-quality (τ ) and generation speed (speedup). DNeo is up-to +20.7% faster than the next-best method (DFlash-2), and is always the fastest method at Temperature=1 (see bold values). DNeo further achieves higher τ than SoTA parallel drafters (up-to +25.1% τ ), while exceeding the draft quality of the SoTA AR drafter EAGLE-3 at Temperature=1 (up-to +21.0% τ ). Notably, DNeo achieves this τ increase solely from architectural improvement, not relying on draft trees [18, 27]. 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. All Rights Reserved. 11 DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding Why DNeo is faster. Speedup is the product of τ , which DNeo raises through the components analyzed in Section 5.4, and the cost of each speculative round. EAGLE-3 exceeds the τ of DNeo on four benchmarks at Temperature=0, yet DNeo is 1.15 to 1.34 faster there, because EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively while DNeo drafts the entire block in one forward pass. Among parallel drafters, the left-to-right causal head makes DNeo round costlier than DFlash round, so DNeo is fastest whenever its τ advantage outweighs this overhead: on every benchmark at Temperature=1 (+32% to +40% τ over DFlash) and on math and code at Temperature=0 (+17% to +19%), but not on GPQA and MT-Bench at Temperature=0 (+10% to +12%). The advantage peaks under sampling because parallel drafter averages each prediction over all plausible predecessors, is less problematic for greedy decoding than for sampling; causal heads correct exactly this mismatch (Section 3), which is also why DSpark and DFlash-2 improve on the τ of DFlash mainly at Temperature=1. 5.3 Higher Throughput The advantage of DNeo in committed tokens per forward (τ ) results in improved throughput, motivating the evaluation of DNeos total generated tokens per second under different concurrency values (batch sizes, B; Table. 3). DNeo exhibits higher throughput than other speculative methods in all settings on the evaluation set (Section 5.1). DNeo also achieves up-to +58% higher throughput (at B=32) than DFlash-2 (Transformers serving). The gap widens under Transformers serving because DNeos throughput advantage there exceeds its advantage in τ : its rounds are also cheaper than those of the baselines, consistent with its leaner prefix-only backbone (Section 4.4). This throughput gap can be attributed to the higher τ DNeo achieves, and the drafters competitive speculative latency (Appendix A.6). high τ also keeps speculation profitable as concurrency grows: at small B, decoding is memory-bound and verifying draft block costs little more than generating one token, but as grows, verification approaches the compute limit of the GPU and every rejected draft token wastes compute that other requests could use. All speculative methods thus lose ground to AR, and DNeo, which commits the most tokens per round, wastes the least. The net result is that DNeo dominates the throughput-speed Pareto  (Fig. 1)  , being the only drafter to maintain throughput parity with the AR baseline at batch size 64 (within 0.1%), while the other drafters fall 10% to 18% below it. sections.title: 5.4.2 DNeo Head
sections.content: Table 6: Causal head ablation. Fused DNeo vs. DFlash-2, and DSpark heads (all heads use projection rank = 256). The DNeo causal head (introduced in Section 4.2) fuses the outputs of the standard low rank DSpark head (Wr, Section 3), and the DFlash-2 score head (Section 4.2) in latent space [8, 22]. Interestingly, the fused head  (Table 6)  exhibits +0.056 τ and +0.141 τ over the DFlash-2 head, and DSpark head alone (respectively), highlighting the complementary inductive biases of the two heads anticipated in Section 4.2: the DSpark head adjusts the full vocabulary but sees only the previous token through low-rank linear map, while the DFlash-2 head is context-aware but only re-ranks the top-16 candidates. The fused head applies context-aware corrections over the full vocabulary, and can therefore promote tokens that the backbone ranks outside its top candidates. sections.title: 5.4.3 Rejection Memory
sections.content: The concurrent work DFlow [41] (Section 3) fuses rejection feature ( ˆfj+1) with masked embeddings [m]j+1, . . . , [m]b on the subsequent draft round using an MLP. However, the DFlow approach ignores the rightmost rejection features ( ˆfj+2, . . . , ˆfb), and compresses rejection feature information into set of fixed mask embeddings. Instead, DNeos rejection memory uses cross-attention to enable each mask token to attend to features of all rejected tokens. As discussed in Section 4.3, these features are informative because the rejected positions overlap those that the next round must draft, and they come at no extra cost for the target model, which already computed their hidden states during verification. Ablating these decisions in Table 7 reveals that fusing rejection features with masked representation (DFlow, no MLP) produces no gain over the (memory-less) DNeo baseline (+0.009 τ ), and gating the fusion with an MLP (DFlow, dMLP = 512) achieves small gain (+0.030 τ ). Notably, combining this fusion with rejection memory (DFlow + rejection memory) produces lower τ than rejection 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc. All Rights Reserved. 14 DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding memory alone (0.034 τ ) showing that mixing masked and rejected representations can serve as quality bottleneck. Fusion adds one rejection feature to every masked embedding regardless of its relevance, perturbing the inputs from which the drafter predicts; in contrast, attention lets each position retrieve only the rejected features it needs. Finding. Rejected proposals are valuable source of context, which are best exploited via cross-attention rather than input-fusion. Table 7: Rejection attention ablation. sections.title: 5.4.4 Layer Selection Protocol
sections.content: Finally, we compare the DNeo protocol with the uniform protocol of DFlash and DFlare (Section 4.5) on DSpark drafter with MoFA encoding. With the DNeo protocol, τ grows with the number of encoded target layers, from 2.481 at = 5 to 2.516 at = 15, whereas with the uniform protocol it decreases, from 2.467 to 2.447; the gap between the two protocols thus widens from +0.014 τ to +0.069 τ as more layers are encoded (appendix Fig. 7). Uniform selection draws each added layer from the full depth of the target model, so many additions come from early layers that carry little drafting signal and dilute the MoFA gate; the DNeo protocol draws every added layer from the later half, so additional layers contribute additional signal. For the same reason, MoFA over all 36 target layers (τ = 2.478) does not outperform the DNeo protocol with only 5 layers: its gate must spread its mass over many uninformative layers (Appendix A.5). Finding. The DNeo protocol encodes more useful target layers, enabling better draft quality under fixed encoding conditions.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper presented DNeo, parallel draft architecture that conditions the drafter on structurepreserving features of the target model and on the features of previously rejected proposals, and corrects its parallel predictions with fused causal head. It showed that dense feature encoders degrade target features through residual mixing, an effect that MoFA, lightweight mixture of target layers, removes by construction. Experiments in realistic serving settings show that the resulting gains in draft quality culminate in up to 1.3 faster generation than state-of-the-art parallel drafters. DNeo illustrates the importance of architectural research in parallel models: rich understanding of which target features matter, and of how to encode them, translates directly into faster lossless inference. 2026 Cerebras Systems Inc.
